measurement.happened:
This week in Ukraine was dominated by three intertwined crises: the Trump-Zelensky public feud, the Starlink/Starlink satellite slowdown, and a fragile diplomatic push toward peace talks, all set against a backdrop of intensifying strikes on both sides.

The US-Ukraine relationship hit a new low. Trump publicly lashed out at Zelensky after Ukraine launched one of its largest drone attacks of the year (over 1,000 drones) at Russia, including a strike on St Petersburg and one on Putin's hometown oil terminal (Reuters, CNN, DW, FT, WSJ, CNBC, Al Jazeera, Bloomberg). Trump waived several Russia sanctions, which Kyiv denounced as an 'encouragement' for Putin (BBC, TV5Monde, CNN, Al Jazeera). He floated a summit with Putin and Xi on Ukraine without Zelensky, saying 'I would do anything to stop the war' (WSJ, CNBC, Bloomberg). Zelensky, in a rare public confrontation, told CNN and Bloomberg that Trump was pushing Ukraine, not Putin, to yield, and that 'if you give something to Putin, he will want everything' (CNN, Bloomberg, DW, TV5Monde). US intelligence sharing with Kyiv was reportedly paused, with Zelensky's adviser telling the BBC that Ukrainians were dying because of it, and Zelensky himself saying partners gave 'no warning' before Russian ballistic strikes (BBC, DW, TV5Monde, FT, Al Jazeera). Zelensky also accused the Pentagon of delaying delivery of Patriot missiles already paid for by European partners (DW, TV5Monde, FT). The Oslo meeting between Zelensky and US envoys Witkoff and Kushner was described as 'positive' and 'productive,' and Zelensky said intelligence sharing was working again by October 21 (AFP, BBC, Bloomberg, TV5Monde). The feud cooled slightly but the underlying tension over who bears the cost of the war and how fast to settle remained raw.

The Starlink/Starshield crisis was the single most dramatic operational story. A Wall Street Journal report revealed that Elon Musk had ordered a slowdown of Starlink service used by Ukraine's military, which hobbled drone operations and communications (WSJ, Reuters, Bloomberg, DW, TV5Monde, CNN, BBC, Al Jazeera). Trump initially said it was a decision for Musk, not the White House (Reuters), then said he would 'fix' the problem (Reuters, CNN). A Republican lawmaker vowed 'consequences' for Musk, and Senator Elizabeth Warren demanded to know who made the decision (CNN). Trump reportedly called Musk to lift the limits (WSJ, Bloomberg). By October 24, Ukraine's defense ministry confirmed Starlink service restrictions had been removed and the connection was 'now stable' (Reuters, BBC, Bloomberg, FT, WSJ, Al Jazeera). The episode exposed Ukraine's deep structural dependence on a single US tech company for its military communications and drone control, a point underscored by Carney (Bloomberg) and a BBC explainer (BBC).

Diplomacy showed genuine, if fragile, progress. Putin agreed to resume three-way peace talks with Ukraine and the US, to be held in early November in Abu Dhabi (Reuters, AP, DW, TV5Monde, Bloomberg, WSJ). US envoy Steve Witkoff met Putin in St Petersburg on October 21, a meeting both sides called positive (BBC, DW, TV5Monde, AFP, CNN). In a highly unusual move, Melania Trump personally brokered a one-city ceasefire in Oleshky, a Russian-occupied Ukrainian city hit by a food crisis, to allow humanitarian aid in (Reuters, AP, BBC, CNN, DW, TV5Monde, Al Jazeera). The Kremlin confirmed the ceasefire and said it was working with Ukraine on evacuation timing (Reuters). Russia and Ukraine also swapped 270 prisoners each (Reuters). Zelensky said he supported the ceasefire and trilateral talks (Reuters, AFP). However, Zelensky remained doubtful about Russia's acceptance of Trump's proposed 'energy ceasefire' (AFP), and the Kremlin signaled it saw 'little to talk about' in the new peace push (BBC).

On the battlefield, both sides kept striking. Russia hit Kyiv with missiles and cluster warheads on October 21-22, killing six and injuring others (Reuters, AP, BBC, CNN, FT, TV5Monde). Russia expanded attacks on energy facilities to western Ukraine (Reuters) and stepped up attacks on Ukraine's digital infrastructure (Reuters). Ukraine fired drones toward Moscow, hit Russian data centers disrupting key services and AI research (AP), and struck Moscow-area airports (DW). A Russian military satellite tracked a US radar satellite used by Ukraine to within tens of meters (TV5Monde). Russia also constructed a new jet-attack drone base in six weeks (TV5Monde). The subterranean battle in Soviet-era pipelines continued (WSJ).

Other notable items: Ukraine's anti-corruption police searched the central bank, with the governor saying there was no link to bank activity (Reuters). Ukraine sought to move customs checks inside the EU to avoid Russian drones (Reuters). Ukraine was set to buy military supplies via a NATO agency (Reuters, FT). The EU leaders planned to discuss 2027 funding for Ukraine at the November 26-27 budget summit (Reuters). A Ukrainian soldier who severed his own foot to survive was rescued in a dramatic drone evacuation, the first-ever battlefield air evacuation by drone (Reuters, AP, DW, Al Jazeera). A Ukrainian man was arrested in northeastern Germany on suspicion of spying for Russia (DW). South Korea repatriated an aid worker and withdrew some embassy staff over a POW transfer dispute (Reuters, AP). Russia detained a German man facing charges for serving in the Ukrainian army (AP, DW). Wheat futures rose on supply fears, and Brent crude held near $110 (Bloomberg).
measurement.expected:
The Oleshky ceasefire will be the most visible diplomatic item next week. I am almost certain that both sides will manage the humanitarian aid corridor and evacuation logistics in Oleshky, as the Kremlin has already confirmed it is coordinating timing (Reuters). The ceasefire is narrow and one-city, so I judge it probable that it holds for the week but also likely that at least one minor violation or dispute over scope will generate headlines. The Abu Dhabi trilateral talks are set for early November, so next week will be dominated by pre-summit positioning: I am almost certain that Witkoff will make another trip to Moscow or a third location to finalize the agenda, and that Zelensky will hold a series of phone calls and possibly another in-person meeting with US envoys to close remaining gaps before the summit. I am probable that both sides will issue statements framing their positions for the talks, and possible that a small additional concession or prisoner exchange is announced as a goodwill gesture before Abu Dhabi.

The Starlink issue is largely resolved for now, with service confirmed stable on October 24 (Reuters, BBC, Bloomberg, FT, WSJ). I am probable that the US Congress will hold at least one hearing or send a formal letter to SpaceX/Musk demanding an explanation, given that two senators and a Republican lawmaker have already raised the issue (CNN, Reuters). I am possible that Musk or SpaceX issues a brief statement, but unlikely that a formal US government inquiry is launched before the midterms. I am almost certain that Ukraine will quietly accelerate its own satellite and communications redundancy plans, and I am probable that European leaders (Carney, EU officials) use the episode to push for a European alternative or joint constellation (Bloomberg).

Military operations will continue at a high tempo. I am almost certain that Russia will keep striking Ukrainian energy and digital infrastructure, especially as winter approaches and Ukraine is racing to secure power supplies (Reuters, DW, TV5Monde). I am probable that Ukraine will launch another large drone package at Russian targets, likely again hitting energy, aviation, or data-center infrastructure deep inside Russia, as it did this week (AP, DW, Al Jazeera, FT). I am possible that a new round of cluster-munition or ballistic-missile strikes on Kyiv occurs, given the pattern of strikes following diplomatic meetings (FT, TV5Monde). I am unlikely that there is a major ground-advance by either side in any single sector in the coming week, as both sides appear to be in a holding pattern ahead of the talks.

The Trump-Zelensky relationship will remain tense but functional. I am probable that Trump makes at least one more public comment pressuring Zelensky to 'make a deal,' possibly in the context of his midterm calculus (Reuters, Bloomberg, CNBC). I am possible that Zelensky responds with a measured public statement, as he did on CNN, but unlikely that he escalates to a full public rupture again before Abu Dhabi. I am almost certain that the US will continue to balance its Ukraine policy against domestic political pressures, with the midterms in the background (Reuters, Bloomberg).

Winter energy anxiety will grow. I am probable that Ukraine announces new measures to secure electricity and gas supplies, including accelerated imports or grid hardening (DW, TV5Monde). I am possible that a significant blackout or power outage occurs in a Ukrainian city due to a Russian strike on infrastructure, generating a spike in public concern. I am unlikely that a full-scale energy crisis breaks out in the next seven days, but the risk is elevated.

Less likely surprises for the week: a surprise announcement that the Abu Dhabi talks are moved up by a few days (possible but not expected); a second city ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump or the White House (possible, given the political optics); a new round of US sanctions or a further waiver that shocks Kyiv (possible); a Russian cyberattack on Ukrainian or European critical infrastructure exploiting the digital-infrastructure theme (possible); a minor Ukrainian drone incident over a NATO country's airspace, like the Lithuania crash this week, triggering a diplomatic row (possible).

Things I would not bet on: a full-scale ground offensive by either side in the next week (unlikely); a sudden collapse of the Oleshky ceasefire within 48 hours (unlikely); a formal US withdrawal from the trilateral process before Abu Dhabi (very unlikely); a major Ukrainian or Russian leadership change or succession crisis (very unlikely); a new US-European trade dispute specifically over Ukraine that dominates the headlines (unlikely); a nuclear-related incident or threat escalation (very unlikely).
emoji_reasons: The Starlink/Starshield slowdown and its resolution was the single most consequential operational and political story of the week, exposing Ukraine's critical dependence on one US satellite system and triggering a transatlantic political fight.

The week saw genuine diplomatic movement: the Oleshky ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump, the 270-prisoner swap, Witkoff's meeting with Putin, and the agreement to hold trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi in early November.

Both sides continued heavy striking: Russia hit Kyiv with missiles and cluster warheads, Ukraine launched over 1,000 drones at Russian cities and energy targets, and the energy and digital infrastructure of both countries took damage.

delta.motion:
Between the two photographs, the Trump-Zelensky feud deepened and became more personal and public. In the first photo Zelensky called Trump's behavior 'painful' and 'betrayed'; in the second he is on CNN and Bloomberg saying directly that Trump is pushing Ukraine, not Putin, to yield, and that 'if you give something to Putin, he will want everything.' Trump escalated from waiving sanctions to floating a three-way summit with Putin and Xi that would exclude Zelensky entirely, and from blaming the Starlink issue on the US military to personally calling Musk to fix it. The feud cooled slightly by October 24 after the Oslo meeting and the resumption of intelligence sharing, but the underlying tension over who bears the cost and how fast to settle remained raw. A new dimension appeared: the Pentagon was accused of delaying Patriot missile delivery that European partners had already paid for, and US intelligence sharing with Kyiv was formally paused before being restored. This was not present in the first photo, where the intelligence gap was an accusation; by the second photo it was a confirmed operational pause with soldiers reportedly dying because of it.

The Starlink/Starshield crisis moved from an ongoing negotiation to a full resolution. In the first photo Ukraine was 'in talks to lift the speed limit' and the front lines were hampered. In the second photo the Wall Street Journal revealed that Musk had ordered the slowdown, Trump initially deflected then intervened personally, Senator Warren and a Republican lawmaker demanded accountability, and by October 24 the defense ministry confirmed restrictions were removed and the connection was 'now stable.' The structural vulnerability of Ukraine's dependence on a single US tech company was highlighted by Mark Carney and a BBC explainer, a layer of analysis absent from the first photo.

Ukrainian offensive action grew substantially. The first photo described a counteroffensive in Donetsk, 'Operation Vivaldi,' and six damaged Russian jets. The second photo describes one of the largest drone attacks of the year, over 1,000 drones, a strike on St Petersburg, a hit on Putin's hometown oil terminal, drones fired toward Moscow, strikes on Russian data centers disrupting AI research, and attacks on Moscow-area airports. The scale and geographic reach of Ukraine's strikes expanded noticeably.

Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure continued and broadened. The first photo had nine regions hit and over a million consumers without power. The second photo shows Russia expanding attacks to western Ukraine and stepping up strikes on digital infrastructure, plus a missile and cluster-warhead attack on Kyiv on October 21-22 that killed six. The pattern of sustained, multi-vector strikes on energy and digital systems was confirmed.

Diplomacy grew from tentative gestures to concrete mechanisms. The first photo had the Pope asking for a truce in Olechky and Hungary-Ukraine resetting ties. The second photo shows Melania Trump personally brokering a one-city ceasefire in Oleshky, a 270-for-270 prisoner swap, Witkoff meeting Putin in St Petersburg, and an agreement to hold trilateral peace talks in Abu Dhabi in early November. The diplomatic channel shifted from multilateral European summits and papal appeals to a more bilateral, US-brokered, personal format.

Several themes from the first photo vanished entirely from the second. The Klitschko protests in Kyiv, the Nord Stream pipeline trial in Germany, the Hungary-Ukraine reset, the Naftogaz gas-reserve milestone, the Arctic seed vault, and the Latvian leader's 'Europe is Zelensky's only ally' framing all disappeared from the headlines. Operation Vivaldi and the Donetsk counteroffensive were not mentioned. The Eutelsat share jump and Poland's foreign minister questioning Musk's politics were gone. In their place appeared: the anti-corruption police searching the central bank; the first-ever battlefield drone evacuation of a wounded soldier; a Ukrainian spy arrested in northeastern Germany; South Korea repatriating an aid worker over a POW dispute; Russia tracking a US radar satellite to within tens of meters; the subterranean pipeline battle; Ukraine buying military supplies through a NATO agency; Ukraine seeking to move customs checks inside the EU; Russia building a jet-attack drone base in six weeks; and the EU planning 2027 funding at a November budget summit. The domestic political and legal stories that dominated the first photo gave way to a broader, more fragmented set of operational, intelligence, and institutional stories in the second.
delta.wind:
The expectation that the Trump-Zelensky rift would 'almost certainly continue to dominate' was correct and the rift was even more intense than forecast. The prediction of 'another public spat' came true in the form of Zelensky's direct CNN and Bloomberg confrontations. The expectation of 'a further sanctions-related headline' was met when Trump waived several Russia sanctions. The forecast that US Congress would 'push back harder, with more hearings or letters' was partially confirmed: Senator Warren demanded to know who made the Starlink decision and a Republican lawmaker vowed 'consequences' for Musk, though a formal hearing was not reported. What the expectation missed was the Oslo meeting between Zelensky and US envoys Witkoff and Kushner, the formal pause and resumption of US intelligence sharing, the Pentagon's alleged delay of Patriot deliveries, and Trump's personal phone call to Musk. The Oslo meeting and the intelligence-sharing resumption were genuine positive developments not in the forecast, and the Pentagon Patriot delay was a new specific grievance that raised the stakes beyond the sanctions and Starlink disputes.

The Starlink/Starshield expectation was that the issue would 'persist in some form' with a 'possible partial fix.' Reality was better: by October 24 the restrictions were fully removed and the connection was stable. This was a complete fix, not a partial one, and it came faster than the 'probable that the issue persists' assessment suggested. The expectation correctly identified the ongoing friction with Musk and SpaceX and the front-line complaints, and the WSJ revelation about Musk's order was consistent with the 'exclusive Reuters report' referenced in the first photo. What was not expected was the level of personal intervention by Trump calling Musk, and the congressional scrutiny (Warren, the Republican lawmaker), which elevated the issue from a bilateral tech-military dispute to a domestic US political one.

The forecast that Russia would 'almost certainly continue and likely intensify strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure' was correct. The prediction of 'at least one major overnight strike wave killing multiple civilians' was met by the October 21-22 Kyiv attack with cluster warheads that killed six. The expectation of Ukrainian refinery strikes was confirmed and exceeded: the 1,000-plus drone attack, the St Petersburg strike, and the hit on Putin's hometown oil terminal went beyond the refinery focus of the first photo. The new dimension of Russian strikes on digital infrastructure and the expansion to western Ukraine were not specifically forecast but were consistent with the 'intensify' expectation.

The EU was expected to 'announce or formalize a new loan or financial package' and Germany to 'move on the debt-brake exemption.' This was only partially met. The EU was planning to discuss 2027 funding at the November 26-27 budget summit, which is forward-looking rather than an immediate announcement. The UK sending more weapons was not specifically confirmed in the second photo. The expectation that European leaders would 'coordinate messaging to present a united front against Trump' was less visible in the second photo than in the first, where the Brussels summit and the Latvian leader's blunt statement had set the tone. The EU was more in planning mode than announcement mode, a slower pace than the forecast implied.

The Nord Stream trial was expected to 'continue with further hearings, witness testimony, and legal arguments' with a 'probable' probability. It did not appear at all in the second photograph. The trial had dropped out of the headline cycle, which was a miss. The expectation that the Klitschko protests would 'generate more headlines' was also not met; the mayor's political challenge vanished from the news. Both of these were domestic or European-legal stories that lost momentum to the more dramatic US-Ukraine and battlefield stories.

The Pope's Olechky truce appeal was expected to generate 'at least one round of statements from both Kyiv and Moscow.' It came in a different form: Melania Trump personally brokered the Oleshky ceasefire, and the Kremlin confirmed it was working with Ukraine on evacuation timing. The papal appeal was effectively superseded by a more direct, US-mediated mechanism, which was not in the forecast. The Hungary-Ukraine reset, expected to produce 'at least one concrete joint statement or meeting,' did not appear in the second photo. The Black Sea shipping issue, expected to 'prompt a NATO or EU discussion,' was not prominently featured.

Oil and energy markets were expected to 'stay elevated' with Brent near or above 110 dollars. This was confirmed: Brent held near 110 and wheat futures rose on supply fears.

Among the 'less likely surprises,' a Trump-Putin phone call or meeting announcement was expected as a possibility. It came in the form of Witkoff meeting Putin in St Petersburg and Trump floating a Putin-Xi summit, which is a close but not exact match. A major Ukrainian breakthrough in Donetsk was not reported. A new Western weapons package from Scandinavia or the Baltics was not mentioned. A second ship incident in the Black Sea did not appear. A dramatic shift in the Nord Stream trial did not occur.

Among the 'things I would not bet on,' the Starlink issue being completely resolved with full speed restoration by October 24 was listed as unlikely. It happened. This was the most notable miss. A full ceasefire or peace deal was not announced, consistent with the forecast. Trump did not publicly reverse the sanctions waiver or apologize. Ukraine did not capture a major Russian-held city. Zelensky did not resign. No nuclear incident occurred. The EU did not formally break with the US. The Oleshky ceasefire is a mini-ceasefire, not a full one, so the 'no full ceasefire' expectation held.

The pattern of errors reveals a tendency to overestimate the persistence of domestic and European-legal stories (Klitschko, Nord Stream, Hungary reset) that faded from the news cycle, and to underestimate the speed and completeness of resolution on the Starlink issue. The expectation also underweighted the personal, almost informal diplomatic channels that emerged (Melania brokering a ceasefire, Trump calling Musk, Witkoff meeting Putin) and overweighted the institutional, multilateral ones (EU summits, papal appeals, budget committees). The forecast treated the EU as an active announcing body when it was actually in a slower planning mode. The intelligence-sharing pause and the Patriot delivery delay were new operational frictions that the forecast did not anticipate, despite the first photo already containing accusations of US intelligence gaps. Overall, the expectation captured the major themes correctly but was too slow in anticipating resolution, too confident in the persistence of secondary stories, and too institutionally framed in a week where personal relationships between leaders became the primary diplomatic channel.
delta.driver: The force pushing Ukraine from the first photograph to the second is the collision between Trump's transactional, personal, deal-making style of diplomacy and Zelensky's need to preserve military capability, sovereign decision-making, and a credible European partnership, all while the war on the ground accelerates. Trump is treating the Ukraine war as a series of bilateral levers he can pull and release: waive sanctions to reward Putin, call Musk to fix Starlink, bring Melania into a back-channel ceasefire, float a three-way summit that excludes Zelensky, and pause intelligence sharing to create pressure. Zelensky is responding with increasing public directness, confronting Trump on open television, accusing the Pentagon of withholding paid-for Patriots, and pressing for a European security architecture that does not depend on one American president's mood. The Starlink episode crystallized the structural vulnerability at the center of this dynamic: Ukraine's military communications and drone operations depend on a single US billionaire's infrastructure, and the only reliable fix was a phone call from the President. The drift toward Abu Dhabi talks, the Oleshky ceasefire, the prisoner swap, and the Witkoff-Putin meeting suggests a tentative recognition on both sides that the war needs a managed endgame, even if the Kremlin signals 'little to talk about' and Zelensky doubts Russia will accept an energy ceasefire. The underlying economic and seasonal pressures are also intensifying: winter is approaching, Russian strikes on energy and digital infrastructure are broadening, Ukrainian gas reserves are high but the grid is under strain, and the EU is still in the slow phase of planning 2027 funding rather than delivering it. The net effect is a week in which the personal relationships between Trump, Zelensky, Putin, and Musk became the primary diplomatic channel, the battlefield expanded in both Ukrainian offensive reach and Russian multi-vector strikes, and the institutional frameworks that were supposed to hold the coalition together, the EU budget process, the US congressional oversight, the NATO procurement pipeline, moved at a slower pace than the crisis demanded.

The motion tells me the dominant force is the collision between Trump's personal, transactional diplomacy and Zelensky's need to preserve military capability and sovereign decision-making. The wind tells me I have been too slow to see resolution (Starlink), too confident in the persistence of secondary stories (Klitschko, Nord Stream, Hungary reset), and too institutionally framed when personal channels dominated. I also underweighted new operational frictions that emerged from existing tensions (intelligence pause, Patriot delay). Correcting for these errors, I weight personal/informal diplomatic channels more heavily, expect faster resolution on operational issues than the default 'it will persist' assumption, and treat the EU as a slower planning body rather than an active announcing one. The pre-Abu Dhabi week will be dominated by positioning: both sides trying to shape the negotiating landscape, the Oleshky ceasefire being tested as a proof-of-concept, and the battlefield continuing to escalate as a form of leverage before talks. The Starlink resolution, while complete, will generate follow-up congressional and political scrutiny. The central bank search and drone evacuation are interesting but secondary stories that the wind says I should not overweight. Winter energy pressure is a structural driver that will keep Russian strikes on energy and digital infrastructure as a near-certain headline. The personal-channel pattern means I should expect at least one more informal diplomatic gesture—another phone call, another back-channel meeting, another personal intervention—rather than a formal institutional announcement. I would not bet on a full ceasefire, a Zelensky resignation, a major ground breakthrough, or a formal EU-US split. I would bet on: continued multi-vector strikes on both sides, at least one personal diplomatic interaction between Trump and Zelensky or Trump and Putin, the Oleshky ceasefire either holding or being tested/expanded, US congressional scrutiny of the Starlink and Patriot issues, and the EU in a coordination-and-planning mode ahead of the November budget summit.

crystal.eli5:
Ukraine is about to enter the most important week before a big peace meeting in Abu Dhabi, where Ukraine, the US, and Russia will sit down to talk about ending the war. But before that meeting, both sides are trying to get the best possible position. Ukraine is launching bigger and bigger drone attacks on Russia, hitting places like St Petersburg and even data centers. Russia is hitting back with missiles on Ukrainian cities and power plants, especially now that winter is coming and everyone needs heat and electricity.

The relationship between US President Trump and Ukrainian President Zelensky is still tense. Trump has been doing things like waiving sanctions on Russia and calling the tech billionaire Elon Musk to fix a satellite internet problem that Ukraine's army depends on. Zelensky is pushing back publicly, saying Trump is pushing Ukraine to give up too much. But they did meet in Norway this week and things cooled down a little. Next week, they will probably talk again by phone or in person, and the main argument will be about who has to make concessions before the Abu Dhabi talks.

In the US, Congress is starting to get involved. Senators are asking questions about the satellite internet mess and about why Ukraine's Patriot missile defenses are being delayed even though Europe already paid for them. In Europe, leaders are quietly planning how to fund Ukraine next year, but they are not going to make a big announcement yet. That is coming in late November. For now, the story is about the personal relationships between the leaders—Trump, Zelensky, Putin, and even Melania Trump, who helped arrange a small ceasefire in one Ukrainian city—and about the bombs and drones that keep falling on both sides as winter gets closer.
